articles.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
articles.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
articles.content:
Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago.

Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams”.

In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago.

To an untrained eye the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world.

Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground. Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood, partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface.

Our new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet.

Valleys, but not from rivers

Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions.

But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few meters) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models.

These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor.

They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water.

What we discovered

To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques.

First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves.

Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside.

The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes.

This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface.

Caves are scientific archives

The results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It shows that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think.

Understanding where voids may exist underground can be important for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works, mitigating geological hazards, and accessing and protecting groundwater resources.

Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and supply water to 10–25% of the global population.

More fundamentally, caves are important scientific archives. Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time.

Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have evolved and adapted in isolation. These are some of the least studied organisms on Earth.

To learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard.

Caves on other worlds

The implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide promising exploration sites for life on other planets.

Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves, including some thought to be related to karst on Mars.

The Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be attractive bases for future human explorers.

How many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too.

Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand.

The authors would like to acknowledge Matthias Leopold from The University of Western Australia; Rok Ciglič, Mateja Ferk, Jure Tičar, Matija Zorn and Matej Jelovčan from the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts (ZRC SAZU); John A. Webb from La Trobe University; Uroš Stepišnik, Matej Dolenec, Primož Miklavc, Tomislav Popit and Andrej Šmuc from the University of Ljubljana; and Jian-xin Zhao from The University of Queensland.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery revealing hidden cave systems beneath Australia's Nullarbor Plain, which has broad implications for environmental science, geological hazard mitigation, groundwater resource management, and astrobiology. The discovery offers a new method to locate caves on Earth and potentially on other planets, contributing to knowledge with tangible benefits for society and future space exploration.

articles.title: An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11465-9An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells
articles.content: All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant technological breakthrough in all-perovskite tandem solar cells that improves both efficiency and stability, which can lead to more effective renewable energy solutions with broad environmental benefits. The detailed description of the molecular innovation and its impact on solar cell performance demonstrates substantial substance and real-world impact.
articles.personality_title: New molecule boosts efficiency and stability in advanced perovskite solar cells
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Perovskite solar cells are a type of solar technology that can convert sunlight into electricity. Tandem solar cells stack two layers to capture more energy, but they often face problems with stability and efficiency, especially where different materials meet.

**What happened** – Scientists developed a special molecule called p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) and added it to a layer in the solar cell. This molecule changes during the cell’s making process to fix defects and reduce harmful chemical reactions. This helps the solar cell work better and last longer. Using this method, they built a solar cell with a power conversion efficiency of 25.4%, which is very high for this type of material. When combined into a full tandem solar cell, the efficiency reached 31.1%, with improved heat resistance and longer operation time.

**Impact** – This improvement is important because it tackles two big challenges: making solar cells more efficient at turning sunlight into electricity and making them more stable over time. The molecule helps fix tiny problems inside the solar cell that usually reduce performance. This means solar panels using this technology could produce more clean energy and last longer, making renewable energy more reliable.

**What's next step** – Researchers will likely work on testing these improved solar cells in real-world conditions and finding ways to produce them at larger scales. This step is necessary to bring this technology from the lab to everyday solar panels used in homes and businesses.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new molecule helps perovskite solar cells convert sunlight into electricity more efficiently and stay stable longer, pushing solar technology forward.

articles.title: Saving Nepal’s wild orchids — in photos
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03475-4Prized for their ornamental and medicinal value, hundreds of orchids are illegally harvested and sold each year. Now, conservationist Reshu Bashyal is leading an effort to protect them.
articles.content:
Bashyal first became involved in orchid research by chance. In 2018, while working on a conifer tree conservation project for non-profit organization Greenhood Nepal in Kathmandu, she visited several regional sites across the country and was often approached by people asking about the demand for orchids in the city. When her team investigated further, it realized that many people living in the villages were harvesting or actively trading the plants.

This illegal trading was often overlooked by authorities, according to Bashyal. Before suggesting a way to stop it, the team had to understand the market — specifically which species were being taken, their conservation status and how the supply chain operated. To do this, it visited orchid trading hubs across Nepal and spoke to harvesters, traders and enforcement officials.

The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife. The Makawanpur region of Nepal is home to orchids, yew trees and a rich diversity of other wildlife.

“The local people provide information on where orchids are harvested, moved, gathered and how much they sold orchids for,” she says. During these visits, the team shared its research and spoke about the importance of conservation, which was well received, she says. “After all, an unsustainable harvesting of the orchids severely threatens local livelihood and income,” she adds.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful conservation effort led by Reshu Bashyal to protect wild orchids in Nepal from illegal harvesting and trade. This initiative addresses biodiversity preservation and sustainable livelihoods, impacting both the environment and local communities. The story provides clear context about the problem, the research conducted, and community engagement, indicating a substantive and significant positive environmental action.

articles.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
articles.summary: Researchers have found that seabirds equipped with audio recorders and GPS trackers can detect ships, offering a way to monitor fishing vessels that are operating illegally
articles.content:
Researchers have found that seabirds equipped with audio recorders and GPS trackers can detect ships, offering a way to monitor fishing vessels that are operating illegally

A northern gannet (Morus bassanus) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales Steve Votier

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

These birds recorded sounds of nearby ships, including some that were not broadcasting their locations. The study found that up to 20% of vessels near these birds were ‘invisible’ to normal tracking methods.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that seabirds can act like natural spies to help catch illegal fishing boats. This method adds valuable information beyond current tracking tools.

articles.personality_title_es: Aves marinas con rastreadores ayudan a detectar barcos pesqueros ocultos

**Contexto** – Muchos barcos pesqueros grandes deben enviar señales que muestran su ubicación. Pero algunos no lo hacen, lo que dificulta saber dónde ocurre la pesca ilegal y cómo afecta a las aves marinas.

Estas aves grabaron sonidos de barcos cercanos, incluyendo algunos que no transmitían su ubicación. El estudio encontró que hasta el 20 % de los barcos cerca de estas aves eran ‘invisibles’ para los métodos normales de rastreo.
